stem: An agent acts on behalf of a logged-in user. Which access model is correct?

options.text: The agent uses a shared service account with broad permissions for reliability
The agent inherits the calling user's permissions, verified at the tool boundary per request
The model decides which records the user may see based on the system prompt
Access is checked once at session start and cached for the session

explanation: Least privilege means an agent never holds a superset of the user's permissions, and entitlement is verified at the tool boundary on each request. Access control must never be delegated to the model, and session-start checks miss mid-session permission changes.
author: legacy

stem: A team deploys a customer-support agent with a system-prompt rule telling Claude to never reveal a customer's full account number. During testing, a cleverly worded support ticket causes the agent to include a full account number in its reply anyway, even though the system-prompt rule was in place the entire time. Which addition would have reliably stopped this from reaching the customer?

options.text: Rewrite the system-prompt rule with stronger wording and more emphatic language
Add an output filter that redacts account-number patterns before the response is sent
Add more few-shot examples of refusals to the system prompt
Rely on the model's built-in safety training without any additional layer

explanation: A system-prompt rule is a request the model can still be talked out of by a sufficiently crafted input; it is one layer, not a guarantee. An output filter that redacts the pattern deterministically before the response ships is a second, independent layer that catches what the first layer missed. Stronger wording and more examples are still prompt-layer fixes with the same failure mode, and relying solely on built-in safety training abandons layering entirely.
author: v1-new

stem: A company's Claude-powered assistants inherit each employee's own permissions, checked once when the employee authenticates at the start of the day. At 10:00 a.m. a manager revokes an employee's access to the payroll system after a role change. At 10:15 a.m. the employee asks her assistant to pull a payroll report, and the request succeeds. What is the root cause?

options.text: The assistant used a shared service account instead of the employee's own identity
Entitlement was cached from a session-start check instead of verified at the tool boundary on each request
The system prompt failed to instruct the assistant to refuse payroll requests after a role change
The manager should have manually revoked the assistant's session token when access was removed

explanation: The setup already has the agent inheriting the user's own permissions, so a shared account isn't the issue. The failure is that entitlement was verified once at login and cached, instead of being checked at the tool boundary on every request; a later revocation had no way to take effect mid-session. A system-prompt instruction can't know about a role change that happened after the prompt was written, and manual token revocation per event doesn't scale into a systemic fix.
